course.title: Probability and Statistics
course.description: Count what can happen. Change a condition, move an outlier, and test what a sample can tell you.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with arithmetic, fractions and the first Maths Foundations lessons.

paragraphs: Probability and statistics both deal with quantities that vary from one occasion to the next, and they work in opposite directions. Probability starts from a setup that is known, such as a pair of fair dice, and says how often each result should turn up: a total of 7 can be made in six different ways, whereas a total of 2 can be made in only one. Statistics starts from results that have already been collected, such as a list of bus delays or the answers to a survey, and asks what they show about whatever produced them.

Between them they let you replace a vague "likely" or "typical" with a number. A probability says how much a new clue should change what you expect, and how quickly the chance of a long run of the same result falls away. A mean, a median and a standard deviation say where a list of measurements sits and how widely it is scattered, and a sample can say something about the whole group it came from, provided that it was chosen without leaving part of the group out. Each of these tools also has a characteristic way of failing, such as counting results that are not equally likely as though they were, or quoting a mean that a single extreme value has dragged away from the rest, and knowing where each one fails is what lets you judge a claim that is made with numbers.
outcomes: You'll be able to find the probability of an event by counting equally likely outcomes.
You'll be able to say how a clue changes a probability, and work out the new value.
You'll be able to multiply the chances of independent events and tell them apart from events that cannot both happen.
You'll be able to find the mean and median of a list and say which one an extreme value moves.
You'll be able to measure how spread out a list is with the range and the standard deviation.

lessons.title: Count what can happen

lead.text: The way out is to list the results so finely that none of them can be split. With two coins, the finest list records what each coin shows, first coin and then second: HH, HT, TH and TT. Each item on this list is called an **outcome**, and since a fair coin has no reason to prefer one face to the other, the four outcomes are **equally likely**, each turning up a quarter of the time. The count of heads is a different matter, because it gathers these four outcomes into groups of unequal size, which is why 0, 1 and 2 are not three equal shares.

A group of outcomes that we ask about is called an **event**. "At least one head" is the event made of HH, HT and TH, and "two tails" is the event made of TT alone. When the outcomes are equally likely, the **probability** of an event is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the number of all the outcomes, so "at least one head" has probability 3/4, or 0.75, and "two tails" has probability 1/4, or 0.25.

The words *equally likely* carry the weight of this rule. Dividing by the number of outcomes treats each outcome as worth the same, and if they are not worth the same the division gives a wrong answer, however carefully the count was made.

reveal.text: Counting heads suggests three possibilities, 0, 1 and 2, and so a probability of 1/3 for each. That is wrong, because the three counts are reached by different numbers of outcomes, and only the four coin-by-coin outcomes are equally likely. The probabilities of 0, 1 and 2 heads are 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4, which add up to 1.

lead.text: Roll one die and then the other, and write the two numbers as a pair, first roll and then second, so that a 2 followed by a 5 is (2, 5). The pair (5, 2) is a *different* result, because there the 5 came first, and each such pair is called an **ordered outcome**.

Both dice are fair and neither affects the other, so every ordered outcome is equally likely, and the counting rule from the coins applies again. It applies correctly only if **every pair is counted, including both orders** of a pair such as (2, 5) and (5, 2).
The figure sets the ordered outcomes out as a grid, with the first roll down the rows, the second roll along the columns, and one cell for each pair.

reveal.text: Coins follow the same rule: 2 results for the first coin, each paired with 2 for the second, give the 4 outcomes HH, HT, TH and TT.

lead.text: Questions about dice usually concern the total of the two rolls, which can be any whole number from 2 to 12. That is eleven totals, and it is tempting to treat them as eleven equally likely outcomes, each with probability 1/11. A total, however, is not one cell of the grid but an [[event|A group of outcomes that we ask about. Met earlier in this lesson.]], made of every cell whose two numbers add up to it, and different totals contain different numbers of cells.

afterFigure.text: Slide the total in the figure and watch the green dots. A total of 2 appears in a single cell, (1, 1), and so does a total of 12, (6, 6), whereas a total of 7 appears in six cells: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2) and (6, 1). Each cell has probability 1/36, so a total of 2 has probability 1/36 while a total of 7 has probability 6/36, which is 1/6. The middle totals are *more likely*, then, not because the dice favour them, but because **more pairs lead to them**.

steps.headline: Finding the probability of a total of 8

workedSteps.text: The event is a total of 8. A first roll of 1 would need a 7 on the second die, which no die can show, so the first roll has to be larger.
The pairs in the event come from taking each first roll in turn and asking which second roll completes the total.
All 36 ordered pairs are equally likely, so the probability of the event is the number of pairs in it divided by 36.

lead.text: Some events collect more than one total. "A total of at least 11" contains the total 11 and the total 12, and its probability comes from counting the pairs behind both.

afterFigure.text: A total of 11 comes from (5, 6) and (6, 5), and a total of 12 from (6, 6), so the event holds 2 + 1 = 3 pairs. With 36 pairs altogether its probability is 3/36, which is 1/12. Adding the pairs first and dividing once is the safest habit, because the denominator then stays the same for every event on the grid: **the number of all the pairs**.

lead.text: Counting the pairs an event leaves out is sometimes shorter than counting the pairs it holds. The pairs that are not in an event make up its **complement**, and every pair is in exactly one of the two, either the event or its complement. In the figure, the green dots mark the event "a total of at least 11", and the cells without dots are its complement.

afterFigure.text: The event holds 3 of the 36 pairs, so its complement holds 36 − 3 = 33, and the probability of a total below 11 is 33/36, which is 11/12. The probabilities 3/36 and 33/36 add up to 1, because together they cover the whole grid, so **the probability of the complement is 1 minus the probability of the event**: 1 − 1/12 = 11/12.

lessons.orientation: Count equally likely outcomes to find a probability, and see why the possible totals of two dice are not equally likely.

blocks.text: Flip two fair coins and count the heads. The count can be 0, 1 or 2, which makes three possible answers, and it is natural to expect each of them to turn up a third of the time. Repeat the flip many times, however, and the three counts turn up at quite different rates.
If what can happen is listed so finely that **every item on the list has the same chance**, finding a chance becomes a matter of counting.

intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea in the course starts from a correct count of what can happen.

recap.keyIdea: When outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in it divided by the number of all the outcomes.

blocks.text: To find a probability, list the outcomes so that each is **equally likely**, as the pairs on a grid of two dice are, count those that belong to the event, and divide by the count of all of them. Totals such as 2 and 7 are *not* equally likely, because they are reached by different numbers of pairs, so a total has to be counted in pairs and not as one item on a list of totals.
When an event holds most of the grid, it is often quicker to count its [[complement|Everything the event leaves out. Met earlier in this lesson.]] and take **1 minus that probability**.

recap.nextHook: Next, a clue about the result removes some of the pairs from the count, and the probability changes with it.

lessons.title: When the condition changes

lead.text: Take the four outcomes of two coins again: HH, HT, TH and TT. The clue "at least one head" rules out TT, which has no head, so the three outcomes HH, HT and TH remain. They keep the same chance as one another, and HH is *one* of the three, so the probability of two heads is now 1/3 and not 1/2.

A probability worked out after a clue is known is called a **conditional probability**, and the clue is the condition: the probability of two heads **given** at least one head is 1/3. The method is the one from the last lesson, in which the outcomes in the event are counted and divided by the number of all the outcomes, with a single change: "all the outcomes" now means **only the outcomes the clue leaves possible**.

A different clue leaves a different list. If you are told that the *first* coin is a head, then HH and HT remain, and the probability of two heads given that clue is 1/2. The two clues sound alike, but they cross off different outcomes, and the count follows the outcomes.

reveal.text: The clue rules out 1, 3 and 5 and leaves 2, 4 and 6. Each of these three is still equally likely, so the probability of a 6 given that the result is even is 1/3, where before the clue it was 1/6.

lead.text: The same idea works on the grid of two dice. Suppose you are told that the first roll was at most 2. Every ordered outcome whose first roll is 3, 4, 5 or 6 is now impossible, which crosses off four whole rows, while the pairs in the rows that remain keep the chances they had, equal to one another.
The clue has not changed any single pair. It has only shortened the list of pairs that could have happened.

reveal.text: Two rows survive, the rows for a first roll of 1 and of 2, with six cells each, so there are 2 × 6 = 12 pairs. Before the clue there were 36, so the clue has cut the list to a third of its length.

lead.text: Keep the clue that the first roll is at most 2, and take the event "the second roll is at most 4". Only two rows are left, and in each of them the cells with a second roll of 1, 2, 3 or 4 match, which is 4 cells per row and 8 in all. The list of possible pairs has 12 pairs, so the probability of the event given the clue is 8/12, or 2/3.

afterFigure.text: The denominator is the part that the clue changes. Dividing 8 by 36 would count pairs that the clue has already ruled out, and it would give an answer to a different question, so **count inside the remaining pairs, and divide by the remaining pairs**. In this example the answer 2/3 is also what 24 pairs out of 36 would give without any clue, because a clue about the first die says nothing about the second.

steps.headline: A second roll of at most 3, given that the first roll is at most 2

workedSteps.text: The clue leaves two rows of the grid, which is 12 pairs, and the event is a second roll of 1, 2 or 3.
Each remaining row still holds all six second rolls, and only some of them count towards the event.
The clue has shortened the list to 12 pairs, so the probability given the clue is the number of pairs in the event divided by 12.

lead.text: Now take the event "a total of at least 8" with the same clue, that the first roll is at most 2. Look at what the remaining pairs can reach: a first roll of 1 can make at most 1 + 6 = 7, and a first roll of 2 can make at most 2 + 6 = 8, so a single pair, (2, 6), is left that qualifies.

afterFigure.text: That makes the probability 1/12 given the clue. Before the clue, 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 of the 36 pairs gave a total of at least 8, which is 5/12, so learning that the first die is small has cut the probability to a *fifth* of its former value. The total depends on the first roll, so **a clue about the first roll bears directly on the event**, and the probability moves.

lead.text: A clue can narrow the list further. If the first roll is known to be 1, only one row of the grid remains, with the six pairs (1, 1) to (1, 6).

afterFigure.text: With one row left, the event "a second roll of at most 3" holds the three cells (1, 1), (1, 2) and (1, 3), so its probability given the clue is 3/6, or 1/2. A tighter clue can therefore move a probability a long way or leave it alone, and here it leaves it at 1/2, since a clue about the first die says nothing about the second.

reveal.text: This equals the probability of a total of 7 before the clue, which is 6/36, since every first roll has exactly one second roll that makes 7. A clue changes a probability only when it makes the event more or less possible than it was.

blocks.text: Flip two fair coins. Before you look, the chance that both land heads is 1 in 4, since HH is one of the four equally likely outcomes. Now suppose you learn that *at least one* of the coins is a head. The natural thought is that the other coin is equally likely to be heads or tails, which would make the chance of two heads 1 in 2, but that is not what the count gives.

intro.whyItMatters: Most real predictions are made after some information is known, so they need a probability that takes the clue into account.

recap.keyIdea: A clue crosses outcomes off the list, and the probability given the clue is counted among the outcomes that remain.

blocks.text: A clue rules out the outcomes that cannot have happened, and the **conditional probability** of an event is found by counting the outcomes of the event that *remain* and dividing by the number of all the outcomes that remain. The denominator is the part that changes: on the grid of two dice, a clue that the first roll is at most 2 leaves 12 pairs, not 36.

A clue changes a probability only when it bears on the event, as a small first roll bears on a large total, and it leaves the probability alone when it says nothing about the event, as it does for the second roll.

recap.nextHook: Next, the second roll that a clue about the first could not move leads to a name and a rule: events that do not affect each other.

lessons.title: Independent repetitions

lead.text: A clue that the first die was at most 2 cut the chance of a total of at least 8 to a fifth of its former value, yet it left the chance of a second roll of at most 3 at 1/2, exactly where it had been.

Two events are **independent** when learning that one of them has happened leaves the probability of the other unchanged. A coin and a die are the plainest case, because nothing the coin does can reach the die: the probability of a 6 is 1/6, and [[given|Used for the clue already known. Met in 'When the condition changes'.]] that the coin showed heads it is still 1/6, since the pairs that remain are heads with each of the six die values and just one of them has a 6. The same holds for repeated flips of one coin, or repeated rolls of one die, where each trial starts afresh.

reveal.text: Each of the 2 coin results pairs with all 6 die results, so there are 2 × 6 = 12 pairs, and none of them is favoured, so all 12 are equally likely. The pair "heads with a 6" is therefore 1 of 12, which makes its probability 1/12.

lead.text: In the list of coin and die pairs, "heads and a 6" is 1 pair out of 12, a probability of 1/12. That is exactly the product of the two chances taken separately, 1/2 × 1/6, and it is no accident: heads takes up half of the list, and inside that half a 6 takes up one sixth, so the pair is a sixth *of a half*.

afterFigure.text: The grid shows the same thing for two dice. Each die is at most 4 with probability 4/6, or 2/3, and the cells where both are at most 4 form a square of 4 by 4, which holds 16 of the 36 pairs and so has probability 16/36, or 4/9. Multiplying the separate chances gives 2/3 × 2/3 = 4/9, the same value. **For independent events, the probability that both happen is the product of their separate probabilities.**

reveal.text: Each die is at most 3 with probability 3/6, or 1/2, and the matching cells form a 3 by 3 square of 9 pairs out of 36. Both routes give 9/36 = 1/4, which is 1/2 × 1/2.

workedSteps.text: For both dice to show at most 2, each die has to land on a 1 or a 2.
The two dice are independent, so the chance that both show at most 2 is the product of the two separate chances.
As a check, the matching cells form a square of 2 by 2, which is 4 of the 36 pairs.

lead.text: If three events are independent, the chance that all three happen is the product of their three chances, and so on for any number. Four flips of a fair coin that all land heads have probability 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/16, since each further flip multiplies the chance by another 1/2.

The flips are independent because an earlier flip does not alter the coin that is flipped next. That is why a run of heads does not make tails *due*: the chance of five heads in a row is 1/32, yet if four heads have already come up, the chance that the fifth is also a head is still 1/2.

Independence is easily confused with a different relation. On one roll of a die, the events "the roll is 1" and "the roll is 2" cannot both happen, because a single roll shows only one number. Events of this kind are called **mutually exclusive**.

The product rule does not apply to them. Each event has probability 1/6, but the chance that both happen is 0, not 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36, because the events are *not* independent: learning that the roll was 1 changes the chance of a 2 from 1/6 to 0.
Independent events can happen together, and do so in the proportion the product gives, whereas mutually exclusive events **never happen together**, and each one rules the other out.

lessons.orientation: Multiply the chances of independent events, and tell independent events apart from events that cannot both happen.

blocks.text: Flip a coin and roll a die. On its own, the coin shows heads with chance 1/2, and the die shows a 6 with chance 1/6. What is the chance of getting *both*, heads and a 6? It cannot be 1/2 or 1/6, because the pair of results is rarer than either one alone, and it cannot be found by adding the chances, which would give 2/3, a larger chance than either.

intro.whyItMatters: Repeated trials, from coin flips to repeated tests, are built by multiplying chances.

recap.keyIdea: For independent events, the chance that all of them happen is the product of their separate chances.

blocks.text: Two events are **independent** when learning that one happened leaves the probability of the other unchanged, and then the chance that both happen is found by *multiplying*: 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12 for heads and a 6, and one more factor of 1/2 for each further flip of a coin. Events that **cannot both happen**, such as a 1 and a 2 on the same roll, are a different relation, and the product rule is not for them.

When an event says "at least one", it is often easiest to find the chance that none of the events happens, which is a product, and take the [[complement|Everything the event leaves out. Met in 'Count what can happen'.]].

lessons.title: Centre and outliers

lead.text: Imagine that the values in a list are amounts of money, put into one pot and then shared out equally. What each share comes to is called the **mean** of the list. To find it, add every value to get the total, and divide the total by how many values there are. For the list 6, 9 and 12 the total is 27, and 27 shared among 3 is 9.

Every value goes into the pot, so **every value affects the mean**. The mean is the number most people have in mind when they say "the average", and it has a useful property: multiplying the mean by the number of values gives the total back, so 9 × 3 is 27.

A second idea of centre ignores how large the values are and asks only where they come in the order. Put the values in order from smallest to largest, and the value in the middle is the **median**, with as many values below it as above it. For 7, 3, 9, 5 and 1 the ordered list is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, so the median is 5.

The ordering has to come *first*. The value in the middle of the list as it was written, 9, is not the median, because 9 is the largest value in the list, and the largest value can never be the middle of an ordered list.

A list of five values has a single middle, but a list of four has two values in the middle, with nothing between them. The median is then taken to be halfway between them, which is the number found by adding the two and dividing by 2. For 1, 3, 5 and 9 the middle pair is 3 and 5, their sum is 8, and the median is 4.

This median, 4, is not one of the values in the list. That is allowed, because the median is meant to mark the point that splits the list into two equal halves, and with an even number of values that point falls *between* two of them.

workedSteps.text: Put the values in order. With four values there are two in the middle.
The two middle values are the second and the third in the ordered list.
The median is halfway between the two middle values, which is their sum divided by 2.

lead.text: Take the list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, for which the [[mean|The total shared out equally. Met earlier in this lesson.]] and the [[median|The middle value once the list is in order. Met earlier in this lesson.]] are both 3. Now drag the largest value along the scale in the figure and watch the two markers. A value that lies far from the rest of the list is called an **outlier**.

afterFigure.text: If the 5 becomes 50, the total rises from 15 to 60, so the mean rises from 3 to 12, which is higher than four of the five values and so describes none of them well. The median is still 3, because the largest value is still the largest however far it travels. **The mean responds to how far a value lies from the others; the median responds only to its place in the order.**

lead.text: Neither centre is the right one in every case, because each answers a different question. The mean answers "what would every value be if the total were shared equally?", so it is the right choice when the total matters.

The median answers "what is a typical value?", and it is the better choice when a few extreme values would drag the mean away from where most of the list lies, as they do with house prices or incomes. When the mean and the median of a list differ a great deal, the difference is itself information, since it points to an outlier or to a long tail of large values.

reveal.text: The mean of these journeys is 39 minutes, longer than four of the five, because the 95 pulls it up. The median, 25 minutes, is the middle journey, which is much closer to the time most of the commuters spent.

blocks.text: A single figure for where the list 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 sits is easy to choose, because 5 lies in the middle of the list and is also what each value would be if the total, 25, were shared out *equally* among the five.
The middle and the equal share are two different ideas, and they give different numbers as soon as **one value lies far from the rest**.

intro.whyItMatters: Most data is reported as a single centre, so you need to know what that number hides.

recap.keyIdea: The mean is the total shared out equally and the median is the middle of the ordered list, and an extreme value moves the mean but not the median.

blocks.text: The **mean** is found by adding every value and dividing by how many there are, so every value, including an extreme one, affects it. The **median** is found by ordering the values and taking the middle one, or the number halfway between the middle two when the count is even, so it depends only on the order.

An outlier therefore pulls the mean towards itself and leaves the median where it was, which is why the mean is the better choice for sharing a total and the median is the better choice for a typical value.

recap.nextHook: Two lists can share the same centre and still look very different, and the next lesson measures how they differ.

lessons.title: Same centre, different spread

lead.text: A centre says where a list sits but not how widely its values are scattered, and the simplest measure of that scatter is the **range**: the largest value minus the smallest. Bus A, which is 10 minutes late on every day, has a range of 10 − 10 = 0, because all of its values are equal. The journey times 22, 25, 25, 31 and 37 minutes have a range of 37 − 22 = 15 minutes.
Its weakness is that it uses only the two ends of the list, and a measure of spread that ignores every other value deserves some suspicion.

Compare the lists 0, 4, 4, 4, 8 and 0, 0, 4, 8, 8. Each totals 20, so each has a mean of 4, and each runs from 0 to 8, so each has a range of 8. In the first list, however, three of the five values sit exactly on the mean, whereas in the second only one does and two values sit at each end of the scale.

The mean and the range cannot tell these lists apart, although they are plainly *not* alike. A measure that does so has to use **every value in the list**, and the natural way to do that is to ask how far each value lies from the mean.

reveal.text: Both lists total 16, so both have a mean of 4. In the first list every value sits on the mean, whereas in the second every value lies 2 away from it, so the centres match and the spreads do not.

lead.text: The distance of a value from the mean is the value minus the mean, positive above the mean and negative below it. For the list 1, 4, 7, whose mean is 4, these differences are −3, 0 and +3. Their sum is 0, and this always happens, because the mean is the point at which the values below and the values above balance, so added together the differences cancel.

To stop them cancelling, each difference is squared first, which gives 9, 0 and 9. Squaring makes every term positive, and it makes a far-off value count for much more than a near one. The average of the squares, 18 ÷ 3 = 6, is called the **variance**. Here the list is the whole group that we want to describe, which is called a **population**, so the squares are averaged by dividing by how many values there are.

The variance has a drawback: it is in squared units, so a list of delays in minutes has a variance in minutes squared, which is hard to relate to the data. Taking the square root puts the measure back into minutes. The **standard deviation** is the square root of the variance, and it can be read as a kind of typical distance of a value from the mean.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the list 1, 1, 1, 9 has a mean of 3. The distances from the mean are −2, −2, −2 and +6, their squares are 4, 4, 4 and 36, which total 48, and the variance is 48 ÷ 4 = 12. The standard deviation is the square root of 12, about 3.46. Drag the last value towards 1 and the standard deviation falls to 0 when all four values are equal, because then **no value lies away from the mean**.

workedSteps.text: The mean of 2, 4, 4 and 10 is 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so the distances from the mean are −3, −1, −1 and +5, and their squares are 9, 1, 1 and 25.
The variance is an average of the four squared distances, and an average starts from their total.
The population variance is the total of the squared distances shared over the number of values.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, which returns the measure to the units of the data.

lead.text: Often a list is only a *sample*, a part of a larger group, and then the mean has itself been estimated from the sample. A sample's own mean sits closer to its values than the true mean of the group does, so squared distances from it come out slightly too small, and dividing by **one less than the count** corrects for that.
For 0, 0, 8, 8 the squared distances total 64. Treated as a whole population the variance is 64 ÷ 4 = 16, and treated as a sample it is 64 ÷ 3, which is about 21.3.

reveal.text: On every day Bus B is exactly 10 minutes from its mean, 0 below it and 20 above it, so its standard deviation is 10 minutes, where Bus A's is 0. The buses share a mean of 10 minutes, and their spreads could hardly differ more.

lessons.orientation: Measure how spread out a list is with the range and the standard deviation, and see why the range alone is not enough.

blocks.text: The delays of two buses over four days, in minutes, are 10, 10, 10 and 10 for Bus A and 0, 0, 20 and 20 for Bus B. Each list totals 40, and 40 divided by four is 10, so the two buses have the same mean delay and a centre alone cannot tell them apart.

Yet the two services are quite different: Bus A is never on time and never very late, whereas Bus B is on time on two days and 20 minutes late on the other two. That difference is the **spread** of the delays.

intro.whyItMatters: A centre without a spread can hide whether a list is steady or wildly variable.

recap.keyIdea: The range uses only the two ends of a list, while the standard deviation uses every value's distance from the mean.

blocks.text: The **range**, the largest value minus the smallest, is quick to find but cannot tell apart lists that share both a mean and a range. The **variance** averages the squared distances from the [[mean|The total shared out equally. Met in 'Centre and outliers'.]], so that every value counts and the distances cannot cancel, and the **standard deviation** is its square root, which returns the measure to the units of the data.
For a whole population the squared distances are averaged by dividing by the count, and for a sample the usual estimate divides by *one less*.
