lessons.title: Samples and populations

lead.text: Every statistical question is about some group. A town with 8,000 homes asks how much its homes spend on heating, and the **population** is all 8,000 homes, because the question concerns every one of them. Visiting all 8,000 would be slow and costly, so a survey visits 300 of them, and those 300 homes are a **sample**: the part of the population that is actually measured.

The population is set by the question and not by who happens to be asked, so a survey that reaches 300 homes still has a population of 8,000. A sample is useful only so far as it resembles the population it was taken from.

reveal.text: The population is every customer the question is about, so both groups belong to it, and 6 + 6 = 12, even though only 6 of them were asked.
The figure shows each customer as a circle, with the morning group in one row and the evening group in the other, and a tick marks the members of whichever sample is chosen.

lead.text: Return to the shop in the opening. Its twelve customers are the population, six who spend £2 and six who spend £8, and the survey that asked only the morning customers took a sample of six from it. The evening customers were never asked, but they are still part of the population, because the question is about the shop's customers and they are customers of the shop. Deciding the population comes first for that reason: until you know whose answer the question needs, you cannot tell whether a sample left anyone out.

The **population mean** uses every member of the population, and the **sample mean** uses only the members in the sample. The population mean is the number the question is really after, and the sample mean is the number a survey can actually find.
When many members share a value, the total is quicker to find by multiplying: a group of 4 members worth 3 and 2 members worth 6 has a total of 4 × 3 + 2 × 6 = 24 over 6 members, so a mean of 4.

steps.headline: The population mean of ten members, five worth 2 and five worth 6

workedSteps.text: The population contains both groups, five members worth 2 and five worth 6, so it has ten members.
Both groups go into the total, each value counted once for every member that has it.
Divide the total by the number of members.

steps.headline: The population mean of the shop's twelve customers

workedSteps.text: Six customers spend £2 and six spend £8, so the population has twelve members.
The total counts each group's value once for every member of that group.
The population mean is the total divided by the number of members, which is 12.

lead.text: The survey in the opening asked only the morning customers. In the figure, choose Morning only: the sample mean is 2, while the population mean is 5. Choose Evening only, and the sample mean is 8. Neither is close to 5, and they miss in opposite directions.

afterFigure.text: A sample whose way of choosing members leaves out part of the population, and so pushes its mean the same way each time, is called a **biased sample**. Asking more people does not help: if the shop had a hundred morning customers and all of them were asked, every one would still spend £2, and the sample mean would still be 2. A survey can reach only the people it has some means of contacting, and if that leaves out part of the population, **a bigger sample from the same method keeps the same bias**.

lead.text: The balanced sample matched the population mean exactly, but that does not make balancing the cure. Here we knew the two groups and their sizes, and in a real survey we do not know in advance which parts of the population matter, so a surveyor cannot balance them by hand. A sample made up of volunteers, or of whoever is easiest to reach, is chosen by the people in it or by convenience, and nothing stops it from leaning one way.

A **probability sample** is chosen by chance, in such a way that every member of the population has a known chance of being selected and that chance is above zero. The method is trusted because of how it picks members, which favours no part of the population, and not because one sample happened to land on the right number.

reveal.text: The total is 6 × 4 + 6 × 10 = 24 + 60 = 84, and 84 ÷ 12 = 7. A sample from either group alone would miss this by 3, giving 4 from the morning customers and 10 from the evening ones.

lessons.orientation: Tell a population from a sample, find a population mean, and see why a large biased sample can still mislead.
lessons.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: A survey reports what a few people said or spent and is read as a statement about everyone, so it can be trusted only as far as the few stand for the many. Consider a shop whose regular customers are six who come in the morning and spend £2 each and six who come in the evening and spend £8 each. A survey that asks only the morning customers finds that every one of them spends £2 and reports £2 as the typical spend, which is true of the people who were asked and untrue of the shop.
The arithmetic in that survey is sound, and the fault lies in **who was asked**, so that asking more morning customers would only repeat the £2.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a population from a sample, find a population mean, and explain why asking more people does not fix a biased sample.
intro.whyItMatters: Nearly every statistic you meet is a sample's answer to a question about a larger group.

recap.keyIdea: A sample is only the part of a population that is measured, and a sample that leaves part of the population out stays biased however large it is.

blocks.text: The **population** is the whole group a question is about, and a **sample** is the part of it that is measured. The population mean divides the total of every member by the number of members, and the sample mean does the same for the members sampled, so the second is only as good as the way the sample was chosen.

A method that leaves part of the population out gives a **biased sample**, and a larger sample from the same method keeps the bias. Selection by chance, with a known and non-zero chance for every member, is what a *probability sample* provides.

questions.prompt: Roll two fair dice, one after the other. How many ordered outcomes are possible?
hints: Count the rows, then the cells in each row.
Each first-roll value can pair with every second-roll value.
Multiply the number of first-roll choices by the number of second-roll choices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 6 first rolls and 6 second rolls, giving 6 × 6 = 36 ordered outcomes.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the 6 first rolls pairs with all 6 second rolls, so you multiply: 6 × 6 is 36.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two dice. Each first roll is paired with every second roll, which combines the counts in a different way.
That is the size of one die. The grid has a cell for each pair, and a pair needs both rolls.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Why does a total of 7 come up more often than a total of 2?
hints: Compare how many cells match each total.

acceptedIdeas: More ordered pairs make 7 than make 2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Six ordered pairs make 7, whereas only (1, 1) makes 2, and each pair is equally likely.

choices.label: The second die tends to land higher than the first
Every possible total is equally likely
More ordered pairs make 7 than make 2

questions.onCorrect: Six pairs make 7 and only one makes 2, so a total of 7 is six times as likely as a total of 2.

misconceptions.feedback: If every total were equally likely, each would have the same number of pairs behind it, but the grid shows one cell for 2 and several for 7.
Neither die tends to land higher, since each shows 1 to 6 equally often. The difference lies in how many pairs add up to each total.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is at least 10? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Count only matching pairs, then divide by all 36 pairs.
List the pairs for totals 10, 11 and 12, including reversed pairs.
There are three pairs for 10, two for 11 and one for 12; divide their combined count by the full grid count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Totals 10, 11 and 12 have 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 outcomes; 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.onCorrect: Three pairs make 10, two make 11 and one makes 12: 6 pairs of 36, which is 1/6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. A probability divides it by all the pairs.
That counts totals, not pairs: 3 out of 11 totals. Totals are not equally likely, so count cells.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is below 10? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Subtract the probability of at least 10 from 1.
The events below 10 and at least 10 partition the full grid.
Subtract the six pairs at least 10 from the full count, then divide by the full count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The complement has 36 − 6 = 30 outcomes, so 30/36 = 5/6.

questions.onCorrect: The event holds the 30 pairs left over, so its probability is 30/36, which is 5/6, or 1 − 1/6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the probability of at least 10. This question asks about the pairs that are left.
That is a count of pairs. A probability divides by all the pairs.

questions.prompt: Two fair four-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 5? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: List the pairs that sum to 5; the changed dice have four sides each.
The pairs (1, 4) and (4, 1) are distinct; include both middle pairs too.
Divide the four matching pairs by four first choices times four second choices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four pairs make 5: (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1). There are 16 pairs, so 4/16 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: Four of the 16 pairs, since the grid is now 4 × 4, and (1, 4) and (4, 1) count separately.

misconceptions.feedback: That count merges (1, 4) with (4, 1) and (2, 3) with (3, 2). They are different ordered outcomes, so each counts.
36 belongs to six-sided dice. How many pairs do two four-sided dice make?

questions.prompt: When can you find a probability by dividing the number of outcomes in the event by the number of all the outcomes?
hints: Think about why dividing by 3 failed for the head counts 0, 1 and 2, and why dividing by 11 failed for the dice totals.

acceptedIdeas: Whenever the outcomes are equally likely
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whenever the outcomes are equally likely

choices.label: Whenever the outcomes can be listed completely
Whenever the outcomes are totals, such as 2 to 12
Whenever the outcomes are equally likely

questions.onCorrect: The division gives every outcome the same weight, so it needs every outcome to have the same chance.

misconceptions.feedback: The head counts 0, 1 and 2 form a complete list as well, and dividing by 3 still gives the wrong chance for each of them. A complete list is not enough on its own.
The eleven totals from 2 to 12 are not interchangeable, since a total of 7 has six pairs behind it and a total of 2 has one. Dividing by 11 gives the wrong chance.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled, one after the other, and you learn that the first roll is at most 2. How many ordered outcomes can still happen?
hints: Count the rows the clue keeps.
Each remaining row still has all six second rolls.
Multiply the number of rows kept by the cells in a row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two first rolls remain, each with six second rolls: 2 × 6 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: Two rows of 6 cells remain, so 12 ordered outcomes can still happen.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the grid before the clue. The clue crosses off whole rows.
That is one row. How many rows does the clue keep?

questions.prompt: Given a first roll of at most 2, what is the probability of a second roll of at most 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Use the count you just made.
Divide the matching pairs by the 12 pairs the clue leaves.
Your count goes on top; the bottom is 12, not 36.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 6 matching pairs among 12 remaining pairs, so 6/12 = 1/2.

questions.onCorrect: Six of the 12 remaining pairs match, so the probability is 6/12, which is 1/2.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 36, the size of the grid before the clue. Divide by the pairs that remain.
That is the number of matching pairs. A probability divides it by the pairs still possible.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the first roll is at most 2. What is the probability that the total is at least 7? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Go through the two remaining rows one at a time.
In the row for a first roll of 1, which second roll makes at least 7? Then do the row for 2.
Add the matches from both rows and divide by 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The matching pairs are (1, 6), (2, 5) and (2, 6), so 3/12 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: Three of the 12 remaining pairs match, (1, 6), (2, 5) and (2, 6), so the probability is 3/12, which is 1/4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the probability without the clue, counted in all six rows. The clue leaves only two rows.
That is a count of pairs. Divide it by the pairs the clue leaves.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the first roll is known to be 1. What is the probability that the total is 7? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Write out the six pairs that remain.
Which second roll makes 7 with a first roll of 1?
Put the number of matches over the number of pairs in the row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only (1, 6) qualifies among the six pairs in the first row: 1/6.

questions.onCorrect: Only (1, 6) makes 7 among the six pairs in the row, so the probability is 1/6.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 36. The clue leaves one row of pairs.
One pair qualifies, but six pairs are still possible.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the first roll is known to be 1. What is the probability that the total is at least 5? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Only the first row remains.
What is the smallest second roll that gives a total of 5 with a first roll of 1?
Count the second rolls from that value up to 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second roll must be 4, 5 or 6: three of the six pairs, so 1/2.

questions.onCorrect: A second roll of 4, 5 or 6 reaches 5, which is three of the six pairs, so 1/2.

misconceptions.feedback: Other second rolls also reach a total of at least 5. List which ones do.
Check the lowest second roll that reaches 5: a smaller one falls short.

questions.prompt: A clue rules out some outcomes. What do you divide by to find the probability given the clue?
hints: Think about which outcomes can still have happened.

acceptedIdeas: The count of outcomes still possible
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The count of outcomes still possible

choices.label: The count of outcomes in the event
The count of outcomes still possible
The count of outcomes before the clue

questions.onCorrect: The clue shortens the list of outcomes, and the event is counted inside the shortened list and divided by its length.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes pairs the clue has ruled out, which cannot have happened.
Dividing the event's count by itself always gives 1, whatever the clue was. The clue has to change the number you divide by.

questions.prompt: Roll two fair dice. What is the probability that both show at most 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Count the 3 by 3 square among all 36 pairs.
Each individual roll passes for three of its six possible values.
Multiply three-sixths by three-sixths, then simplify the resulting fraction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each die passes with probability 3/6 = 1/2, so both pass with probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: Each die passes with probability 1/2, and 1/2 × 1/2 is 1/4. The 3 by 3 square holds 9 of the 36 pairs.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one die alone. Both dice have to pass, so the chance is smaller than that.
Adding the two chances overshoots. Both must happen at once.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that both show at most 2? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Each individual probability is the one you just found.
The matching cells form a two-by-two square.
Divide the area of that square by the full count of 36 pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each die passes with probability 2/6 = 1/3, so both pass with probability 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9.

questions.onCorrect: Each die passes with probability 1/3, and 1/3 × 1/3 is 1/9, which matches the 4 cells of the 2 by 2 square.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one die. Both dice must pass.
That adds the two chances. Both must happen, so combine them another way.

questions.prompt: Why may you multiply the two chances?
hints: Independence concerns how a condition affects a probability.

acceptedIdeas: Knowing one event does not change the probability of the other
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Events are independent when learning that one occurred does not change the other's probability, when the conditional probability is defined. Equivalently, their joint probability is the product.

choices.label: Knowing one event does not change the probability of the other
The events cannot happen together
Both events have probability one half

questions.onCorrect: Learning that one event happened leaves the other's chance unchanged. That is why the chances multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: Events that cannot happen together are mutually exclusive, which is different.
Independence is about whether one result changes the other's chance, not how large the chances are.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that at least one of them shows above 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Subtract the chance that both rolls are low from 1.
Its complement is both rolls at most 3.
Subtract nine matching low-low pairs from the full grid and divide by the full count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both at most 3 has probability 1/4; the complement is 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

questions.onCorrect: Both dice at most 3 has probability 1/4, so at least one above 3 has probability 1 − 1/4, which is 3/4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance that both are low. The question asks about the pairs left over.
That is one die alone. Either die can be the high one.

questions.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed independently. What is the probability of two heads? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: List the ordered coin outcomes.
Keep HT and TH separate when listing the possible pairs.
Divide the one heads-heads outcome by the full count of outcomes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each coin shows heads with probability 1/2, so both do with probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: Each coin shows heads with probability 1/2, and 1/2 × 1/2 is 1/4, the same as HH among four outcomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one coin. Both coins have to show heads.
HH, HT, TH and TT are four results, not three. Keep HT and TH separate.

questions.prompt: On a single die roll, the events "the roll is 1" and "the roll is 2" are which kind of pair?
hints: Can both events occur in one roll?

acceptedIdeas: Mutually exclusive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The events are mutually exclusive: one roll cannot be both 1 and 2. They are not independent, because knowing that 1 occurred makes the probability of 2 zero.

choices.label: Identical
Mutually exclusive
Independent

questions.onCorrect: One roll cannot be both 1 and 2. Knowing the roll was 1 makes a 2 impossible, so the events are not independent.

misconceptions.feedback: Independent events can happen together, and learning one leaves the other unchanged. Here a 1 makes a 2 impossible.
These are two separate events with different outcomes. Ask whether both can occur on one roll.

questions.prompt: The last 5 becomes 25, so the values are 2, 4, 4, 5 and 25. What happens to the mean and the median?
hints: Compare the total with the position of the middle value.

acceptedIdeas: The mean rises and the median stays 4
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Replacing 5 with 25 increases the total and hence the mean. The sorted middle observation is still 4, so the median is unchanged.

choices.label: The mean rises and the median stays 4
Both remain unchanged
The median rises to 25

questions.onCorrect: The mean uses every value, so it rises. The median only needs the order, so it stays.

misconceptions.feedback: The total changes when one value changes, so the mean cannot stay put.
The median is a place in the sorted list, not the biggest value.

questions.prompt: Five people put £2, £4, £4, £5 and £5 into a pot and share it out equally. How much does each get, in pounds?
hints: Add all five values, then divide by five.
There are five observations, including repeated values.
Divide the sum of all observations by their count.
questions.onCorrect: The pot holds £20, and 20 shared among the five is £4 each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole pot. Share it among the five people.
That averages just two of the amounts. Put the whole pot together, then share it equally.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 2, 4, 4, 5 and 25?
hints: Find the middle position after sorting.
An odd-sized sorted dataset has a single middle position.
With five values, take the third value of the sorted list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The values are already in order, and the third of five is 4.

questions.onCorrect: The third of the five values, 4, is the median. The mean of this list is 8, dragged up by the 25.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 25 drags up. The median is the middle value.
That is the largest value. The median is the middle one in size order.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 10, 2, 6 and 4?
hints: Average the middle pair, not the endpoints.
The even-sized sorted list has two middle positions.
Take the average of the second and third values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In order: 2, 4, 6, 10. The middle pair is 4 and 6, so the median is (4 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: The middle pair 4 and 6 adds to 10, and half of 10 is 5, which is the median.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean. The median averages only the middle pair.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of 1, 3, 3, 5 and 18?
hints: Every observation contributes to the total.
There are five values, so the denominator is five.
Add the five values and divide the sum by five.
questions.onCorrect: The total is 30, and 30 shared among 5 values is 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle value, the median. The mean uses every value.
That is the total. Share it among the values.

questions.prompt: A list has an even number of values. Which statement about its median is true?
hints: An even-sized dataset has two middle positions.

acceptedIdeas: It is halfway between the two middle values
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is halfway between the two middle values

choices.label: It is halfway between the two middle values
It must be one of the values in the list
It must be the same as the mean

questions.onCorrect: With an even number of values the middle falls between two of them, so the median is their average and may not be in the list.

misconceptions.feedback: Take 1, 3, 5 and 9, whose median is 4. The list has no 4 in it, so the median does not have to be one of its values.
The mean and the median can differ a great deal. For 1, 2, 3 and 100 the mean is 26.5 and the median is 2.5.

questions.prompt: Compare the lists 4, 4, 4, 4 and 2, 2, 6, 6. How do their means and their spreads compare?
hints: Work out each mean. Then look at where the points sit.

acceptedIdeas: The same mean, different spread
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both lists average 4. The first has no deviation from it, while the second lies two below or above.

choices.label: Identical distributions
The same mean, different spread
Different means, the same spread

questions.onCorrect: Both lists total 16, so each has a mean of 4. The first has every value on the mean, and the second has every value 2 away from it.

misconceptions.feedback: Work out each mean first: do the lists really differ there?
The same mean does not put the points in the same places. Compare where they lie.

questions.prompt: What is the range of 2, 2, 6 and 6?
hints: Subtract the minimum from the maximum.
Repeated values do not change which endpoints are smallest and largest.
Subtract the smallest endpoint, 2, from the largest endpoint, 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The largest value is 6 and the smallest is 2; the range is 6 − 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The range is the largest minus the smallest, so the repeats make no difference.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two extremes. Compare them another way.
That is the largest value. Compare it with the smallest.

questions.prompt: What is the population standard deviation of 2, 4, 4 and 10?
hints: What is the mean? How far is each value from it?
Square each distance, add the squares and divide by four.
The squares average to the variance. Take its square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The variance is 9, and its square root is 3.

questions.onCorrect: The variance is 9, so the standard deviation is its square root, 3, which sits between the near values, 1 from the mean, and the far one, 5 from it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the variance. The standard deviation is its square root.
That is the total of the squared distances divided by two. Use the count of values.

questions.prompt: What is the population variance of 0, 0, 8 and 8?
hints: Square each distance from the mean of 4.
The mean is 4; compute the squared distance of each 0 and each 8.
Add those four squared distances and divide by the count of four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is 4, every squared distance is 16, so the variance is 64 ÷ 4 = 16.

questions.onCorrect: Every value lies 4 from the mean, so each squared distance is 16, and the variance is 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the standard deviation. The variance is the average of the squared distances, before the root.
That is the total of the squares. Divide by how many values there are.

questions.prompt: What is the range of 3, 4, 4, 7 and 13?
hints: Only the two endpoints determine the range.
The interior values do not affect a range calculation.
Use only the maximum and the minimum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The maximum minus the minimum is 13 − 3 = 10.

questions.onCorrect: The largest value is 13 and the smallest is 3, so the range is 13 − 3, which is 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the largest value. The range compares it with the smallest.
That adds the extremes. The range is their difference.

questions.prompt: A list is a whole population, and a second list is a sample from a larger group. What differs in how the variance is calculated?
hints: Is every member of the group in the list, or only some?

acceptedIdeas: The population divides by its count, the sample by one less than its count
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The population divides by its count, the sample by one less than its count

choices.label: The population divides by one less than its count, the sample by its count
Both divide by the count, so nothing differs
The population divides by its count, the sample by one less than its count

questions.onCorrect: A sample's mean is estimated from the sample itself, which makes squared distances slightly small, so the usual sample estimate divides by one less than the count.

misconceptions.feedback: Check which list has a mean that was estimated from its own values. Squared distances from that estimated mean come out slightly too small.
A sample's mean is worked out from the same values that are then measured against it, which makes its squared distances come out slightly too small, so the calculation has to change.

questions.prompt: The shop's customers are six morning shoppers and six evening shoppers, and only the morning ones were asked. How many members does the population have?
hints: Who is the question about: only the people asked, or all the customers?
The evening shoppers belong to the population even though nobody asked them.
Add the morning group's size to the evening group's size.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The population has both groups: 6 + 6 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: The population is everyone the question is about, so both groups count: 6 + 6 is 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one group, the people who were asked. The population has both groups.

questions.prompt: The shop has six customers who spend £2 and six who spend £8. What is the population mean, in pounds?
hints: Use every member of the population.
Count each of the two group values six times.
Use the total divided by the number of members.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 6 × 2 + 6 × 8 = 60, and 60 ÷ 12 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: The total of 60 shared among the 12 members is 5, a mean of £5 that neither group alone gives.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each counts once for every member.
That is the morning group alone. The population has both.

questions.prompt: A sample matches the population mean in one constructed example. What follows?
hints: One observed match cannot establish a general guarantee.

acceptedIdeas: It shows agreement here, without guaranteeing agreement elsewhere
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Agreement in this constructed sample is evidence about this case only. It does not guarantee that another sample or another measured quantity will agree.

choices.label: It proves there is no sampling error
It proves the method is unbiased in every population
It shows agreement here, without guaranteeing agreement elsewhere

questions.onCorrect: One match shows agreement here. It does not guarantee agreement elsewhere.

misconceptions.feedback: One match in a made-up example cannot prove a method works in every population.
Sampling error is the chance gap between a sample and the population. One match does not remove it.

questions.prompt: A shop has six morning customers who spend £4 and six evening customers who spend £10. What is the population mean, in pounds?
hints: The two groups have equal size.
The group sizes are equal, so both contribute the same weight.
Use the total of both groups divided by the combined group count.
questions.onCorrect: The total of 84 shared among 12 members is 7, which is 3 from each group's value.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each counts for every member of its group.
That is the morning group alone. The population has both.

questions.prompt: A survey meant for a whole city reaches only weekday visitors to one gym. What is the main limitation of its results?
hints: Compare the target population with the people the survey can reach.

acceptedIdeas: Residents who never visit that gym have no chance of being asked
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Residents who never visit that gym have no chance of being asked

choices.label: Not enough people were asked, which a larger gym sample would fix
Gym visitors do not belong to the city's population at all
Residents who never visit that gym have no chance of being asked

questions.onCorrect: Residents who never visit that gym on weekdays cannot be reached, and asking more gym visitors does not bring them in.

misconceptions.feedback: Ask who a bigger group of gym visitors would still leave out. A larger sample from the same method keeps the same bias.
Gym visitors who live in the city are residents like any others, so they belong to its population. The trouble lies in who else the survey can reach.

questions.prompt: Which description fits a probability sample?
hints: Ask who or what decides which members end up in the sample.

acceptedIdeas: Members are chosen by chance, and each has a known chance above zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Members are chosen by chance, and each has a known chance above zero

choices.label: Members are picked by the surveyor so that the sample matches the population
Members are chosen by chance, and each has a known chance above zero
Members are volunteers, or whoever is easiest for the survey to reach

questions.onCorrect: The chances can differ between members, so long as each is known and above zero.

misconceptions.feedback: A surveyor cannot know in advance which parts of the population matter, so picking by hand can still lean one way. What counts is how members are picked.
Volunteers put themselves forward and the easiest to reach are picked for convenience, so nothing stops either group from leaning one way.

questions.prompt: Why sort the values before picking the middle one?
hints: Is the middle of the list as written the middle in size?

acceptedIdeas: The middle means the middle in size, not in the order written
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The median is the middle in size order. The order the values were written down tells you nothing about that.

choices.label: Sorting changes the median
The mean needs the values in order
The middle means the middle in size, not in the order written

questions.onCorrect: The median is the middle in size order, so the list must be in that order first.

misconceptions.feedback: Sorting only puts the values in order. It doesn't change them.
The mean doesn't depend on order. It is only the median that does.

questions.prompt: The ordered list is 2, 4, 6, 10. What is the sum of its two middle values?
hints: Which two values are the middle pair of four?
Add the second value and the third.
Add the two middle values only.
questions.onCorrect: The two middle values 4 and 6 add up to 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds all four values. Only the middle pair goes in.

questions.prompt: Five houses sell for these prices, in thousands of pounds: 180, 190, 200, 210 and 720. A report needs one figure for the typical sale. Which figure suits that purpose?
hints: Work out the mean and the median, then compare each with the five prices.
Ask which of the two would change if the 720 became 1,000.

acceptedIdeas: The median, 200, because the one very large sale does not pull it away from the rest
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The median, 200 thousand pounds. The mean is 300, which is higher than four of the five sales because the 720 pulls it up, whereas the median is the price of the middle sale and the 720 does not move it.

choices.label: The median, 200, because the one very large sale does not pull it away from the rest
Either one, because the mean and the median of a list are always close together
The mean, 300, because it uses every sale

questions.onCorrect: The median is the price of the middle sale, 200 thousand pounds, and it stays there however large the 720 becomes, whereas the mean of 300 is higher than four of the five sales.

misconceptions.feedback: The mean is 300, which is higher than four of the five sales, because using every sale means that the 720 pulls the figure up. A typical sale is better described by a figure that one extreme value cannot move.
Here the mean is 300 and the median is 200, which differ by 100 thousand pounds because the 720 raises the mean and leaves the median where it was.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 1, 3, 3, 5 and 18?
hints: Are the values in order?
Five values: which position is the middle?
Take the third value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The values are in order, and the third of five is 3.

questions.onCorrect: The third of the five values is 3, and the 18 does not move it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which uses every value. The median is the middle one.
That is the largest value. The median is the middle in size order.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 1, 2 and 9?
hints: Is the list in order?
Three values: which position is the middle?
Take the middle value of the sorted list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sorted middle of three values is 2.

questions.onCorrect: The middle of the sorted list. The 9 does not move it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 9 drags up. The median is the middle value.

questions.prompt: A coin is flipped twice. HT means heads, then tails. How many different results can you get, counting HT and TH as different?
hints: Write them out: start with the ones that begin with heads.
Two begin with H. How many begin with T?
List HH, HT, then the two that begin with T.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: HH, HT, TH and TT: 4 results.

questions.onCorrect: 4: HH, HT, TH, TT. Listing every result is where probability starts.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts how many heads you might see: none, one or two. HT and TH are different results, so list the order too.
Each flip has two sides, but the flips go together. List what the pair of flips can show.

questions.prompt: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is not 12? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: How many of the 36 pairs make a total of 12?
Only one pair makes 12. How many pairs are left over?
Count the pairs that are not 12, then divide by all the pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only (6, 6) makes 12, so 36 − 1 = 35 pairs do not: 35/36.

questions.onCorrect: The 35 pairs other than (6, 6) make 35/36, which is the same as 1 − 1/36.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the probability of a total of 12. The question asks about every other pair.
That treats the eleven possible totals as equally likely. Count pairs instead: some totals have more than one.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. How many ordered pairs make a total of 8?
hints: Start with a first roll of 2. What second roll makes 8?
Work along the first rolls. Does a first roll of 1 have a partner?
The pairs run (2, 6) to (6, 2). Count them.
questions.onCorrect: Each first roll from 2 to 6 has exactly one partner, so there are 5 pairs.

misconceptions.feedback: A first roll of 1 would need a second roll of 7, and no die shows 7. Check which first rolls have a partner.
That leaves out a pair. Both (2, 6) and (6, 2) count, and so does the pair with two equal rolls.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 8? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Use the count you just made.
Divide the pairs that make 8 by all the pairs.
Your count goes on top; the bottom is every ordered pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 pairs out of 36: 5/36.

questions.onCorrect: 5 of the 36 equally likely pairs, so 5/36, or about 0.139.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 6 ÷ 36, which does not use the count of pairs that make 8.
That divides by 11, the number of different totals. Divide by the number of ordered pairs instead.

questions.prompt: Two fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of exactly one head? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: List all four results.
Which of the four results have exactly one head?
Put the number of those results over the number of all four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: HT and TH are 2 of the 4 outcomes, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.onCorrect: HT and TH are 2 of the 4 outcomes, so the probability is 2/4, which is 1/2.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts a single outcome, but more than one of the four has exactly one head.
That treats the head counts 0, 1 and 2 as equally likely. The four coin-by-coin outcomes are the ones that are equally likely, so count those.

questions.prompt: You flip a coin and roll a die. One result is heads with a 3. How many different results are there?
hints: List the results that start with heads. How many are there?
Each coin result pairs with every die result.
Heads pairs with six die results, and tails does too.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 coin results × 6 die results = 12.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the 2 coin results pairs with all 6 die results, so you multiply: 2 × 6 is 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sides of the coin and the die. Each coin result pairs with every die result, as in a grid.
That counts only the results with heads. Tails pairs with the die results as well.

questions.prompt: One fair die is rolled. What is the probability that it shows at most 2? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Which values are at most 2?
Count how many of the six values qualify.
Put the number of qualifying values over the number of values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two of the six values, 1 and 2, qualify: 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.onCorrect: The values 1 and 2 qualify, which is 2 of 6, so the probability is 1/3.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts values. A probability divides by the six possible values.
Count 1 and 2 both: two values qualify, not one.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of tails and a number above 4? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Find each chance alone: tails, then a number above 4.
Tails is one of two results. Which die numbers are above 4?
The two chances are independent, so combine them with the product rule.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tails is 1/2 and a number above 4 is 2/6 = 1/3; the events are independent, so 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.

questions.onCorrect: Tails has probability 1/2 and a 5 or 6 has probability 1/3, so together 1/2 × 1/3 is 1/6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 5/6, which comes from adding 1/2 and 1/3 and also from taking 1/6 away from 1. Both events have to happen together, which is rarer than either one alone, so the answer must be smaller than 1/3.
That is the chance of a number above 4 alone. The coin has to show tails as well.
That is the chance of tails alone. The die has to show a number above 4 as well.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped three times. What is the probability of three heads? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: One flip shows heads with probability 1/2. Does the first flip change the second?
The flips are independent. How many chances do you multiply?
Multiply the chance for each flip together.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each flip is heads with probability 1/2, so three heads has probability 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

questions.onCorrect: Each flip contributes a factor of 1/2, and 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 is 1/8.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one flip. All three have to be heads, which makes the chance smaller.
That is two flips. There is a third to include.
Adding the chances gives more than 1, which cannot be a probability. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of tails and an even number? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Find the chance of tails alone, then of an even number alone.
Even numbers on a die are 2, 4 and 6. What fraction is that?
The two are independent, so combine the two chances as the lesson says.
questions.onCorrect: Independent chances multiply: 1/2 × 1/2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the two chances. Both must happen.
Adding the chances overshoots. Both must happen at once.

questions.prompt: One die is rolled. Are “shows 1” and “shows an even number” mutually exclusive?
hints: Is the number 1 odd or even?

acceptedIdeas: Yes: one roll cannot be both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1 is odd, so a roll cannot show 1 and an even number together.

choices.label: Yes: one roll cannot be both
No: both can happen on one roll

questions.onCorrect: Yes. One roll cannot be both, so they are mutually exclusive.

misconceptions.feedback: The first number is odd. Ask whether a roll can be odd and even at once.

questions.prompt: Bus A is exactly 10 minutes late on each of four days. Bus B is late by 0, 0, 20 and 20 minutes. What is the range of Bus B's delays, in minutes?
hints: Which day was Bus B's best, the least late?
Its worst day is the most late. How many minutes is that?
Take the smaller from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The largest delay is 20 and the smallest is 0, so the range is 20 − 0 = 20 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: The worst day is 20 minutes late and the best is 0, so the range is 20 − 0, which is 20 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Bus B's mean. The range compares its two extreme days.
That is the total lateness over four days. Compare only the best and worst days.

questions.prompt: Why square each distance from the mean?
hints: Add the distances 1 − 3, 1 − 3, 1 − 3 and 9 − 3. What do you notice?

acceptedIdeas: Distances below the mean would cancel distances above it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Distances below the mean are negative and above are positive, so they cancel. Squares are never negative.

choices.label: Distances below the mean would cancel distances above it
Squaring makes every number smaller
The mean is always a square

questions.onCorrect: Distances below the mean cancel distances above. Squares are never negative, so they all count.

misconceptions.feedback: Squaring a number above 1 makes it bigger. Think about the signs of the distances.
The mean can be any number. Think about what happens to negative distances.

questions.prompt: The squared distances are 9, 1, 1 and 25. What is their total?
hints: Add all four squared distances, including both of the 1s.
9 + 1 + 1 is 11, and the 25 is still to come.
Add 25 to 11.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The squared distances 9, 1, 1 and 25 total 36.

questions.onCorrect: The squared distances add up to 9 + 1 + 1 + 25, which is 36, and the single far value, 10, supplies 25 of it.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the squared distance 1 only once. Both values of 4 lie 1 from the mean, so 1 is added twice.
That adds the distances 3, 1, 1 and 5 without squaring them. Add the squares.

questions.prompt: A population of four values has squared distances from its mean of 9, 1, 1 and 25. What is its population variance?
hints: Divide the total by how many values there are.
Four values, so divide by four.
Take the total of the squares and share it over the four values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total of 36 over four values gives a variance of 36 ÷ 4 = 9.

questions.onCorrect: The total of 36 shared over the four values gives a variance of 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the squares. Divide by how many values there are.
Dividing by one less is for samples. This list is the whole population.

questions.prompt: Bus B is late 0, 0, 20 and 20 minutes, a whole population. What is its population standard deviation, in minutes?
hints: Find the mean first. How far is each day from it?
Square that distance, then average the squares.
The average of the squares is the variance. Take its square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is 10, every squared distance is 100, the variance is 100, and the standard deviation is 10.

questions.onCorrect: Every day is 10 minutes from the mean, so the variance is 100 and the standard deviation is 10 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the variance. Take its square root to return to minutes.
That is the range. Use every day's distance from the mean instead.

questions.prompt: What is the population standard deviation of 3, 3, 9 and 9?
hints: Find the mean first.
Every value is the same distance from the mean. Square that distance.
The squares average to the variance. Its square root is the standard deviation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is 6, every squared distance is 9, so the variance is 9 and the standard deviation is 3.

questions.onCorrect: Every value lies 3 from the mean of 6, so the variance is 9 and the standard deviation is 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the variance. The standard deviation is its square root.
That is the mean. Spread is about distance from it.

questions.prompt: The squared distances from the mean of a whole population are 2, 4 and 6. What is the variance?
hints: The variance is the average of the squared distances.
Add the squared distances, then divide by how many there are.
Divide the total of the squares by three.
questions.onCorrect: The variance is the average squared distance from the mean.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the squares. Divide by how many values there are.
That divides by two. Use the count of values.

questions.prompt: A shop has 12 customers. Six are morning shoppers who each spend £2. Six are evening shoppers who each spend £8. You ask only the morning shoppers. What average spend do you find?
hints: Who does your survey reach?
Every morning shopper spends the same amount.
The average of identical amounts is that amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All six morning shoppers spend £2, so the average is £2.

questions.onCorrect: £2. The survey was honest and still missed half the customers.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the average of every customer. Your survey only reaches the morning shoppers.
That is the evening shoppers. They were not asked.

questions.prompt: A town has 5,000 homes, and a survey about heating costs visits 200 of them. How should the two groups be described?
hints: Which homes were actually visited?
Is the group the question is about the whole town, or only part of it?

acceptedIdeas: The 200 homes are the sample and the 5,000 homes are the population
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The question is about all 5,000 homes, so they are the population, and the 200 homes that were visited are the sample.

choices.label: The 200 homes are the population, because they are the homes that were measured
The 5,000 homes are the sample, because the survey is about all of them
The 200 homes are the sample and the 5,000 homes are the population

questions.onCorrect: The sample is the part that was asked, 200 homes, and the 5,000 homes are the population.

misconceptions.feedback: The survey is about all 5,000 homes, which makes them the population. A sample is only the part that is actually visited, here 200 homes.
The population is set by what the question is about, which is every home in the town, and not by which homes happen to be measured. The 200 homes measured are the sample.

questions.prompt: Why count both groups when finding the population mean?
hints: Who does the population include?

acceptedIdeas: The population is everyone the question is about
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The population is everyone the question is about

choices.label: A sample has to include both groups
The population is everyone the question is about
The larger group counts for more in a mean

questions.onCorrect: The population is the whole group the question is about, so every member of both groups goes into the total.

misconceptions.feedback: Here both groups have five members, so neither counts for more. Ask whose values the question needs.
This line is about the population, not the sample, and a sample does not have to be balanced.

questions.prompt: Six customers spend £2 and six spend £8. What is the total spend of all of them, in pounds?
hints: Six members are worth the first amount each.
Find six lots of each value, then add.
Add six times the first value to six times the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six 2s plus six 8s total 12 + 48 = 60.

questions.onCorrect: Six customers at £2 make £12 and six at £8 make £48, which is £60 in all.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each is counted once for every member.

questions.prompt: Another shop has six morning customers who spend £1 and six evening customers who spend £7. A balanced sample takes three customers from each group. What is the sample mean, in pounds?
hints: Add the six sampled values.
Three lots of the first value plus three lots of the second.
Divide the total by the six members sampled.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 3 × 1 + 3 × 7 = 24, and 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: The six sampled customers spend £24 in all, and 24 shared among 6 is £4, which is also the mean of all twelve of the shop's customers.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each is counted three times.
That is the total. Divide by the six members sampled.

questions.prompt: A population has four members worth 3 and four worth 9. What is its mean?
hints: Use every member of the population.
Four lots of each value, added.
Divide the total by the number of members.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 4 × 3 + 4 × 9 = 48 over eight members; the mean is 6.

questions.onCorrect: The total of 48 shared among 8 members is 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each counts for every member of its group.
That is one group alone. The population has both.

questions.prompt: Two coins are flipped. You are told that at least one landed heads. How many of the four results HH, HT, TH and TT could still have happened?
hints: Cross out any result with no heads in it.
Which of the four has no heads at all?
Take TT out of the list and count what is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: TT has no heads, so HH, HT and TH remain: 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The clue crossed out TT and left a shorter list. That list is where the next probability lives.

misconceptions.feedback: TT has no heads, so it cannot match the clue. Cross it out.
Check HH as well as the mixed results: which of the four fit the clue?

questions.prompt: Why divide by 12 and not by 36?
hints: Which pairs can still have happened once you know the first roll?

acceptedIdeas: The clue rules out the other pairs, so only 12 can have happened
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Once the first roll is known to be at most 2, only the pairs in those two rows are possible.

choices.label: Twelve is always the denominator
Dividing by 36 gives a smaller number, which is safer
The clue rules out the other pairs, so only 12 can have happened

questions.onCorrect: The clue rules out the other pairs, so only the pairs in the surviving rows can have happened.

misconceptions.feedback: The denominator is whatever the clue leaves possible, and that changes with the clue.
A probability is not chosen to be small. It has to count what is actually possible.

questions.prompt: How many of the 12 remaining pairs have a second roll of at most 3?
hints: Count the cells in one remaining row with a second roll of at most 3.
Each of the two remaining rows has the same cells matching.
Multiply the matches in one row by the number of rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three matching second rolls in each of two rows gives 3 × 2 = 6 pairs.

questions.onCorrect: Each remaining row has three cells with a second roll of 1, 2 or 3, and 3 × 2 is 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one row. Two rows survive.
That is every remaining pair. Count only those with a second roll of at most 3.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the first roll is at least 5. What is the probability that the total is at least 10? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: The clue leaves the rows for a first roll of 5 and of 6.
Go through each remaining row and find which second rolls reach 10.
Add the matches from both rows and divide by the pairs that remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rows 5 and 6 give 12 pairs; (5, 5), (5, 6), (6, 4), (6, 5) and (6, 6) total at least 10, so 5/12.

questions.onCorrect: Rows 5 and 6 leave 12 pairs, and five of them total at least 10, so the probability is 5/12.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 36. The clue leaves only two rows.
That is the number of matching pairs. Divide it by the pairs the clue leaves.

questions.prompt: A die is rolled and you are told the result is even. How many results can still have happened?
hints: Think of the faces of a die.
Cross off the faces that are odd.
Count the faces that remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The even results are 2, 4 and 6: 3 results.

questions.onCorrect: The even results 2, 4 and 6 remain, so three results can still have happened.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the list before the clue. The clue rules some of the results out.
More than one even result is possible, so the clue leaves more than one result.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 8, 2, 9, 4 and 3?
hints: Put the values in order first. Which is smallest?
Five values, so the middle is the third once they are in order.
Write them from smallest to largest, then count along to the third place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In order the values are 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, so the median is the third, 4.

questions.onCorrect: In order the values are 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, and the third of the five is the median.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle of the list as written. The median is the middle once the values are in size order.
That is the mean, which uses every value. The median is the middle one in order.

questions.prompt: Five houses sell for these prices, in thousands of pounds: 180, 190, 200, 210 and 720. What is the median price, in thousands?
hints: Are the prices in order? Which is in the middle?
Five values: the middle is the third.
The third price in order is the one you want.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The prices are in order, and the third of five is 200.

questions.onCorrect: The middle sale of the five, in order, is 200, so the median price is £200,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 720 drags up. The median is the middle price.
That is the largest price. The median is the middle one in size order.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Which total comes up more often, 4 or 6?
hints: Count the cells in the grid that make each total.
List the pairs that make each of the two totals, then compare how many there are.

acceptedIdeas: A total of 6
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A total of 6

choices.label: A total of 4
A total of 6
Both come up equally often

questions.onCorrect: Five pairs make a total of 6 and only three make a total of 4, so out of the 36 equally likely pairs a 6 comes up five times for every three times a 4 does.

misconceptions.feedback: A total of 4 is made by (1, 3), (2, 2) and (3, 1). Count the pairs that make the other total and compare the two counts.
Each total is a group of cells in the grid, and the groups are not all the same size. Count the cells behind each total.

questions.prompt: A die is rolled once. Event A is "the roll is even" and event B is "the roll is 5". How are A and B related?
hints: Ask whether an even roll and a roll of 5 can both happen on the same roll.
Then ask what learning that the roll was 5 does to the chance that it was even.

acceptedIdeas: A and B are mutually exclusive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A and B are mutually exclusive

choices.label: A and B are mutually exclusive
A and B are independent
A and B are both mutually exclusive and independent

questions.onCorrect: A roll of 5 is odd, so A and B can never happen together, and learning that B happened takes the chance of A from 1/2 to 0. Events that rule each other out are therefore not independent.

misconceptions.feedback: Independent events can happen together and leave each other's chance unchanged. Check whether an even roll and a roll of 5 can both happen on the same roll.
Learning that the roll was 5 takes the chance of an even roll from 1/2 to 0, which is a complete change. Independent events leave each other's chance as it was.

questions.prompt: Five commuters spent 22, 25, 25, 28 and 95 minutes travelling to work, the 95 on a day when the railway was closed. A report needs one figure for the typical journey. Which figure suits that purpose?
hints: Work out the mean and the median, then compare each with the five journeys.
Ask which of the two would change if the 95 became 150.

acceptedIdeas: The median, 25 minutes, because the 95 does not pull it up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The median, 25 minutes, because the 95 does not pull it up

choices.label: Either one, because both describe the centre of the list
The mean, 39 minutes, because it uses every journey
The median, 25 minutes, because the 95 does not pull it up

questions.onCorrect: The median is the middle journey, 25 minutes, and it stays there however long the 95 becomes, whereas the mean of 39 is longer than four of the five journeys.

misconceptions.feedback: The two figures here are 39 and 25, which are far apart, so the choice matters. Ask which of them the 95 has pulled away from the journeys most commuters made.
The mean is 39 minutes, which is longer than four of the five journeys, because the 95 pulls it up. Ask whether that describes a typical journey.

questions.prompt: Another route, Bus C, is late by 3, 11, 8 and 15 minutes on four days. What is the range of its delays, in minutes?
hints: Which day was Bus C's best, the least late?
Its worst day is the most late. How many minutes is that?
Take the smaller from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The largest delay is 15 and the smallest is 3, so the range is 15 − 3 = 12 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: The worst day is 15 minutes late and the best is 3, so the range is 15 − 3, which is 12 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the largest delay. The range compares it with the smallest.
That adds the two extremes. The range is their difference.
That is the mean delay, which uses every day. The range compares only the best and the worst day.

questions.prompt: A school has 900 pupils. To find out how its pupils travel to school, a teacher asks the 30 pupils in her own class. How should the two groups be described?
hints: Which pupils does the question about travelling to school concern?
Which pupils were actually asked?

acceptedIdeas: The 30 pupils are the sample and the 900 pupils are the population
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 30 pupils are the sample and the 900 pupils are the population

choices.label: The 30 pupils are the sample and the 900 pupils are the population
The 30 pupils are the population and the 900 pupils are the sample
The 30 pupils are the sample and the other 870 pupils are the population

questions.onCorrect: The question is about how all 900 pupils travel, so they are the population, and the 30 who were asked are the part of it that was measured.

misconceptions.feedback: The population is the whole group the question is about, which is every pupil, and a sample is only the part of it that was asked. Ask which of the two groups is part of the other.
The 30 pupils who were asked belong to the population as well, since the question is about every pupil. The population leaves nobody out.

flashcards.front: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled independently. What is the probability of a total of 3?
flashcards.back: The pairs (1,2) and (2,1) give 3, so the probability is 2/36 = 1/18.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pairs (1,2) and (2,1) give 3, so the probability is 2/36 = 1/18.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the event consisting of all outcomes outside event A?

question.prompt: Two fair spinners are independent. What is the probability that their numbers sum to 5? Give a fraction or decimal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 3 × 4 = 12 equally likely ordered pairs. (1,4), (2,3) and (3,2) sum to 5, giving 3/12 = 1/4.

question.prompt: These four values are the entire population. What is their population variance?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No rain on either day has probability (3/4) × (3/4) = 9/16. Its complement is 1 - 9/16 = 7/16. Independence is a stated model assumption, not a claim about real weather.
